clue.text: Astonish someone who has forgotten it is now April?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to give someone an unexpected shock

definitions.text: someone who has forgotten it is now April?
definitions.meaning: second meaning, read literally: for a person who has lost track of the date, the season of spring arrives as a shock

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is read twice: once as the idiom for startling someone, once literally as the spring season taking a forgetful person unawares.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to present someone with something unexpected, so it is a fair synonym for astonish.

clue.text: Novel in eg German urges me to translate

indicators.note: translating turns words into a different form, so these letters are put into a new order

explanation.surface: A German-language novel is being urged on the reader for translation.
explanation.walkthrough: The Greengage Summer is a 1958 novel by Rumer Godden, set in France; the answer drops the article.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the title of a well-known English novel, so the answer is an example of the definition.

clue.text: Such an MND performance would be fundamentally defective

definitions.text: Such an MND performance would be fundamentally defective

parts.words: Such an MND performance would be fundamentally defective
parts.note: MND is A Midsummer Night's Dream, whose comic weaver is called Bottom; a staging with that character missing would lack its base, literally and figuratively

explanation.walkthrough: Bottom is the weaver in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream; a production without him lacks him, and 'fundamentally' plays on the bottom as the base.
explanation.definitionFit: Without a base or limit is the ordinary sense, here read as missing the character Bottom.

clue.text: PM remains, about to resign

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for remains is placed around the other piece

parts.note: ash is what remains after burning
to quit a job is to resign from it

explanation.surface: A Prime Minister stays put, on the point of resigning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'remains' looks like a verb (the PM stays), but it is the noun, burnt remains.
explanation.definitionFit: H. H. Asquith was the British Prime Minister from 1908 to 1916, so he is an example of a PM.

clue.text: Endlessly played up in small island

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from the bottom to the top, so backwards
without its end, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: toyed means played, as with a toy

explanation.surface: Something played without stopping, up on a little island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endlessly' takes the last letter off TOYED to leave TOYE, and 'up' turns that round.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyot (or ait) is a small island in a river, a word found mostly on the Thames.

clue.text: Items Spanish composer has to leave — the centre cannot hold: why not?

definitions.text: the centre cannot hold: why not?

parts.note: Manuel de Falla was a Spanish composer
to part is to leave or go away

explanation.surface: Objects and a Spanish composer have to go, quoting Yeats's poem about collapse.
explanation.walkthrough: Yeats's poem The Second Coming says 'Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold', so the answer is the reason the centre fails.
explanation.definitionFit: The line from Yeats gives the cause: everything disintegrating explains why the middle gives way.

clue.text: What's that Henry and Eleanor film? Write hint online to get sorted

definitions.text: What's that Henry and Eleanor film?

indicators.note: sorting puts things into a new order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks the name of a film and is told to type a hint into a search engine.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1968 film stars Peter O'Toole as Henry II and Katharine Hepburn as Eleanor of Aquitaine.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the title of the film about King Henry II and his queen Eleanor of Aquitaine.

clue.text: I usurp, so false as a Pretender

definitions.note: a phrase standing for the adjective: being as a pretender is, not genuine

indicators.note: false means fake or not genuine, so these letters are a counterfeit arrangement to be reordered

explanation.surface: A claimant to the throne admits to usurping it, and so being bogus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'false' looks like the definition but is the anagram signal; the Pretender, a Stuart claimant to the British throne, is the bogus thing defined.
explanation.definitionFit: A pretender's claim is not genuine, and spurious means counterfeit or illegitimate.

clue.text: Sailor's chant you cut short — very funny

indicators.note: cut short means the last letter is lopped off

parts.note: ho ho is a laugh, often said to mean very funny

explanation.surface: A sailor's song is interrupted with a sarcastic laugh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut short' drops the last letter of YOU to leave YO.
explanation.definitionFit: The cry is the traditional sea shanty refrain of pirates and sailors, as in 'and a bottle of rum'.

clue.text: Turn aside and plunge to the right

parts.note: RT is a standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A swimmer swerves and dives off to the right.
explanation.definitionFit: To divert something is to change its course, a synonym for deflecting.

clue.text: Straighten out the seaweed?

parts.note: tangle is a kind of kelp, so removing it would literally be un-tangling, as well as straightening out knots

explanation.walkthrough: Tangle is a name for large brown seaweed such as kelp, so the word can be read as UN + TANGLE, the opposite of seaweed.
explanation.definitionFit: To free something from knots is to smooth or disentangle it.

clue.text: Gone in the end, slug with eyes on stalks

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, so only that is taken

explanation.surface: A slug that has gone off, with its eyes on stalks.
explanation.walkthrough: Slugs really do carry their eyes on stalks, which hides the idiom for being eagerly excited.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone eagerly excited or amazed, which is what agog means.

clue.text: Not very masculine offshoot, strangely rhymes with 'boot'

indicators.note: strangely means in an odd arrangement, so these letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A poet notes that an unmanly son's name oddly rhymes with boot.
explanation.definitionFit: A son overly attached to his mother is seen as unmanly, so he is a soft offshoot of the family.

clue.text: At first, organising lunch etcetera is problematic: there's a roll for us

indicators.note: a problematic arrangement is a messed-up one, so the letters are shuffled
at first means the opening letter of each of the next words

explanation.surface: Organising lunch and all the rest is a headache, though there's a bread roll for us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At first' takes O and L from 'organising lunch'; with ETCETERA that makes the letters to shuffle. The 'roll' is the electoral roll, not bread.
explanation.definitionFit: Voters as a body are listed on the electoral register, so we, the voters, are on that roll.

clue.text: A quiet Greek and you turning very pale

parts.note: sh is the call for quiet

indicators.note: turning means turning round, so the old word for you is read backwards

parts.note: ye is an old form of you

explanation.surface: A quiet Greek and you go white as a sheet.
explanation.definitionFit: Ash grey is the colourless shade of ash, used of someone who has turned extremely pale.

clue.text: Sticker back on a container

indicators.note: back means reversed, so the cricket word is read the other way

parts.note: in cricket the leg side is also called the on side

explanation.surface: A label is stuck back on a jar.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the leg side of the field is also the on side, so 'on' gives LEG.
explanation.definitionFit: Gelatin is used as glue and setting agent, so here it is a thing that makes things stick.

clue.text: Di not Jo's written in diary every day

indicators.note: Di not Jo means Di is put where Jo was, a swap

explanation.surface: It was Di, not Jo, whose words appeared in the daily diary.
explanation.definitionFit: Diurnal means daily or happening in daytime, so it fits each day.

clue.text: His 'n' hers formal wear? No, just his

definitions.text: His 'n' hers formal wear? No, just his

parts.words: His 'n' hers formal wear? No, just his
parts.note: the name sounds like a woman's frock plus a man's top, but it is only a man's formal top worn with a dinner jacket

explanation.walkthrough: The answer looks like two garments, a woman's dress and a man's shirt, but it is a single man's garment for evening wear.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a man's formal shirt, worn with black or white tie, not a pair of his-and-hers clothes.

clue.text: Fine fabric that looks best green

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a fine linen or cotton cloth
second meaning: grass in a garden, best when green

explanation.walkthrough: One meaning is a sheer cloth, the other the grass in front of a house.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawn is a thin linen fabric and also a mown grass area in a garden.

clue.text: One helping the cast dance and become exhausted, losing some energy

parts.note: a prom is a formal dance

indicators.note: losing means one letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: to peter out is to become exhausted
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A cast member dances until worn out, running low on energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing some energy' drops an E from PETER to leave PTER.
explanation.definitionFit: In the theatre the prompter feeds forgotten lines to actors, so helps the performers.

clue.text: Holding front of dress beside bustle

indicators.note: holding means containing, so one word goes around the letter
front means the first letter is taken

explanation.surface: A seamstress holds the front of a dress next to its bustle.
explanation.walkthrough: A bustle looks like the padded back of a Victorian dress, but here it means commotion.
explanation.definitionFit: A to-do is a commotion or fuss, the sense of bustle as busy activity.

clue.text: Engineers wooden fret

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a British army corps

explanation.surface: Engineers fit a wooden fret, as on a guitar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fret' suggests the ridge on a guitar neck, but it is the verb to worry.
explanation.definitionFit: To repine is to be discontented or grieve, a synonym of worrying.

clue.text: Rise and call out an email command

indicators.note: calling out means speaking, so the words sound like the answer

parts.note: a Send is the command that dispatches an email, so an email command is A SEND

explanation.surface: A user gets up and shouts a command to send an email.
explanation.definitionFit: To ascend is to go up or climb, the sense of rise as a verb.

clue.text: Republican in training not yet a lawyer

indicators.note: in means put inside, so the letter goes into the rearranged letters
training shapes something into a new form, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A Republican is still in training and not yet a qualified lawyer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'training' rearranges NOT YET to TTONEY, 'in' puts R into it, and A goes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: An attorney is a legal representative, the American term for a lawyer.
